0.0.n: Points to something nearby and comes directly before a noun.

0.1.n: Refers to the side of the body, near the armpit.

0.2.n: Links 脇 to ところ, identifying which area to look at.

0.3.n: Refers to a particular spot on the figure.

0.4.n: Marks the area as the object of 見る; English uses look at.

0.5.n: 見る in its て-form plus いただく humbly presents the listener’s looking as a favor.

0.6.n: Introduces what the listener will notice upon looking.

1.0.n: Signals that the speaker has just noticed something.

1.2.n: A casual alternative to 何か, used when the speaker has not identified what they see.

1.3.n: Polite form of いる, used for living beings, including the being depicted here.

1.4.n: Invites the listener to share or confirm the observation.

2.2.n: 合掌する in its て-form links this pose to the description that follows.

2.4.n: Names one of the visible body parts being described.

2.5.n: Joins 頭 and 手 into a single list.

2.6.n: Japanese nouns do not usually distinguish singular from plural; the prayer pose indicates two hands.

2.7.n: Marks the head and hands as the subject, but the speaker leaves the thought unfinished.

3.0.n: Introduces a spontaneous reaction to what the speaker sees.

3.2.n: Used alone as an informal exclamation of admiration or surprise.

4.0.n: The name of the Buddha’s mother, followed here by the title 夫人.

4.1.n: A respectful title for a married woman, attached here to Maya’s name.

4.2.n: Links Lady Maya to the body part that belongs to her.

4.3.n: Refers to the side of Maya’s body, from which the Buddha is depicted emerging.

4.4.n: Marks the starting point of the birth or emergence.

4.5.n: A respectful name for Shakyamuni Buddha, with both お and 様 adding honor.

4.6.n: Identifies the Buddha as the one being born.

4.7.n: 生まれる in its て-form plus いる presents the birth as unfolding in the depicted scene.

4.8.n: Turns the preceding description of the birth into something the artwork depicts.

4.9.n: Marks the birth scene as what is depicted by 表した.

4.10.n: Plain past form of 表す; here it leads into a description whose following noun is not included.

5.0.n: An exclamation of interested surprise; the long vowel draws out the reaction.

6.0.n: Modifies ところ and expresses surprise at the unusual place of birth.

6.1.n: Refers back to Maya’s side as the unexpected place of emergence.

6.2.n: Marks the point of origin and leaves the rest of the thought hanging.

7.0.n: 生まれる in its て-form plus きました, polite past of 来る, emphasizes coming into the world.

7.2.n: Locates the birth in the present moment of the scene being viewed.

7.3.n: Emphasizes 今, stressing that this is the very moment of birth.

0.lit: If we have you look at this side area,
0.tip: 見ていただく politely invites the listener to look by treating their action as a favor.

1.lit: Oh, something is there, isn't it?
1.tip: います treats the figure being depicted as a living being rather than an ordinary object.

2.lit: Yes. Pressing hands together in prayer, the head and hands...
2.tip: The final が marks the subject, but the speaker stops before saying what the head and hands are doing.

3.tip: すごい can stand alone as a complete reaction, much like Wow in English.

4.lit: Depicted the scene of the Buddha being born from Lady Maya’s side,
4.tip: Everything from 摩耶夫人 through 生まれている describes 様子: the scene being depicted.

5.tip: へえー expresses interested surprise, often when learning or discovering something new.

6.tip: Ending with から leaves the action unstated because the birth is already understood.

7.lit: He came to be born, now precisely.
7.tip: 今まさに comes after the verb for emphasis, highlighting the exact moment represented in the scene.
